verses.1:
For the choirmaster. A Maskil of the sons of Korah. + 42:1 In many Hebrew manuscripts Psalms 42 and 43 constitute one psalm. Maskil is probably a musical or liturgical term; used for Psalms 32, 42, 44–45, 52–55, 74, 78, 88–89, and 142. 
 As the deer pants for streams of water,
 so my soul longs after You, O God.
verses.2:
My soul thirsts for God, the living God.
 When shall I come and appear in God’s presence? + 42:2 Or and see the face of God?
verses.3:
My tears have been my food
 both day and night,
 while men ask me all day long,
 “Where is your God?”
verses.4:
These things come to mind as I pour out my soul:
 how I walked with the multitude,
 leading the festive procession to the house of God
 with shouts of joy and praise.
verses.5:
Why are you downcast, O my soul?
 Why the unease within me?
 Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him
 for the salvation of His presence.
verses.6:
O my God, my soul despairs within me.
 Therefore I remember You
 from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon —
 even from Mount Mizar.
verses.7:
Deep calls to deep
 in the roar of Your waterfalls;
 all Your breakers and waves
 have rolled over me.
verses.8:
The LORD decrees His loving devotion by day,
 and at night His song is with me
 as a prayer to the God of my life.
verses.9:
I say to God my Rock,
 “Why have You forgotten me?
 Why must I walk in sorrow
 because of the enemy’s oppression?”
verses.10:
Like the crushing of my bones,
 my enemies taunt me,
 while they say to me all day long,
 “Where is your God?”
verses.11:
Why are you downcast, O my soul?
 Why the unease within me?
 Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him,
 my Savior and my God.

metadata.source: Derived from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB). Missing verses restored from the Textus Receptus tradition for completeness.
